answers.question: How does a piece become a king, and what can it then do?
answers.answer:
A piece becomes a king when it reaches the farthest row from its owner (the opponent's king row), at which point it is promoted immediately by crowning it with a second piece [checkers 4.1]. If promotion happens on the final jump of a capturing chain, the turn ends there and the piece does not continue jumping that turn [checkers 4.1].

Once crowned, a king gains abilities an ordinary piece lacks: it can move one square diagonally in any direction, forward or backward [checkers 4.2], and it captures the same way as a regular piece (jumping an adjacent opponent's piece into the empty square beyond), but it may jump forward or backward and chain multiple jumps in any mix of directions [checkers 4.3]. This is a major upgrade, since ordinary pieces may only move and capture forward [checkers 2.4]. The compulsory-capture rule still applies to kings [checkers 4.3].

answers.question: How do you win each game?
answers.answer:
**Checkers:** You win when your opponent has no legal move at the start of their turn — either because you've captured all their pieces, or because their remaining pieces are all blocked [checkers 5.1, checkers 2.1]. A draw can occur instead if neither side can force a win [checkers 5.2].

**Tennis:** A "game" is won by reaching 40 and winning another point, unless both players reach 40, in which case play continues until one player gets a two-point lead [tennis 5.1]. Games accumulate into sets (won by reaching six games with a two-game margin, or via a tiebreak at six-all) [tennis 5.3, tennis 5.4], and sets accumulate into a match win [tennis 2.1].
